cards.title: Amazon P&L anatomy for a first-year FBA product (revenue, product cost, referral fee, FBA pick & pack)
cards.summary: How to build a per-month Amazon FBA profit statement and which cost lines to subtract to know whether a product actually earns money.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a product can hit your target margin before you commit to an order, or reconciling a month's revenue against real profit.
steps: Model the four cost blocks the source uses for every month of an FBA product: (1) product cost from the supplier, (2) Amazon referral fee at 15% of sale price, (3) FBA pick-and-pack (fulfillment) fee charged per unit shipped by Amazon, and (4) advertising (PPC) spend plus any quality-control or inspection costs.

Work a real ratio from the source's example rather than an assumption: in a month with about $9,500 revenue, the seller paid roughly $2,600 in product cost, $1,400 referral fee and $1,200 FBA fees, landing about $4,000 profit — i.e. roughly 40% of revenue kept in a good month.

Separate months by whether inventory was available all month. In the same example, a month with only partial inventory ($15,000 revenue) produced about $5,500 profit, and the seller's own estimate was that a full 30 days would have produced $45,000+ revenue — so judge product economics only on fully-stocked months.

Treat these figures as one seller's case study, not a benchmark. Referral percentage, FBA fee sizes and profitability vary by category, size, weight and price point; verify current Amazon fee schedules before signing off on a sourcing decision.
Use the model as a go/no-go gate on sourcing: if the landed product cost plus 15% referral plus estimated FBA fee leaves too little for ad spend and returns, the product fails before launch.
caveats: All numbers are a single beginner case study, not an average or guarantee; fee rates and FBA prices change and must be checked against current Amazon documentation.
Revenue in a month with a stockout understates true demand — do not read stockout months as demand signals.

cards.title: Inventory availability as the core driver of Amazon revenue growth
cards.summary: Why stockouts are the most expensive recurring mistake for a scaling Amazon seller and how reorder timing should be planned around demand, not around minimums.
cards.use_when: Planning reorder quantities and reorder timing for a product that is selling faster than expected, or diagnosing a revenue drop after a good month.
steps: Track units sold per week against units on hand and units already in production, so a stockout is visible weeks before it happens rather than discovered when the listing goes quiet.

Note the source's pattern: the featured seller ran out three times in his first year and estimated the cost at roughly $100,000; months two, three, five and six all collapsed toward zero because there was nothing to ship, then recovered only when inventory landed.

When numbers (costs, sell-through, ad efficiency) support the product, order more on the next cycle rather than ordering the same small quantity out of fear — the source's own advice to his past self was to put more money into inventory once the numbers look good.
If you do stock out, treat the recovery as a launch again: you lose ranking momentum and must rebuild with ads and conversion work, so avoid repeating the gap.

The presenters note even experienced sellers make this mistake (one of them expected to stock out on a new electrolytes product), so build the buffer into the plan rather than relying on discipline alone.
caveats: Running out of inventory was framed as the single biggest mistake in this case study, costing ~$100,000 — this is one seller's estimate, not a general benchmark.
Over-ordering to avoid stockouts ties up cash and creates aging-inventory risk; the source's advice is to scale once the numbers justify it.

cards.title: Qualify manufacturer capacity, not just MOQ, before scaling orders
cards.summary: How asking suppliers about maximum monthly output prevents the growth ceiling that cost the case-study seller about $20,000.
cards.use_when: Negotiating with a supplier before or during a scale-up, or when choosing between staying with an existing manufacturer and adding a second one.
steps: Ask every supplier two questions, not one: the MOQ (minimum order quantity) and the maximum quantity they can produce and ship in a single month.
Compare that monthly maximum against your projected monthly unit demand at your goal ad spend and ranking, using sell-through from your best fully-stocked month as the input.

If the ceiling is below projected demand, either split production across a second manufacturer before you need it, or line up the alternative early — the seller in the source changed manufacturers only after he was already out of stock and lost months of sales.
Treat manufacturing capacity as a launch-planning input, not a later operational fix: the source attributes at least $20,000 of lost profit to asking only about minimums.
caveats: Source-specific figure (~$20,000) from one seller's first year; your exposure depends on product, margin and seasonality.
Splitting production across suppliers adds consistency and QC risk that must be managed.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Quality control between sample and bulk production run
cards.summary: Why approving a sample is not approval of the production run, and how a low-cost third-party inspection protects reviews.
cards.use_when: Arranging an overseas production run, or diagnosing a spike in returns, poor reviews or listing complaints after a new batch arrives.
steps: Treat the sample as a demonstration of what is possible, not a guarantee of what bulk will be: the source's seller loved his sample, then received bulk units of inconsistent quality because he did not verify the run.
Hire an independent quality-control agent to inspect the bulk goods before they ship — the source states you can hire someone in China for around $100 to check product quality.
Budget QC as a standard line item on every production run, especially after any change of manufacturer.

Track return rate and review sentiment as your measurement of QC: in the source case, bad quality produced returns and bad reviews, and the presenter frames reviews as currency on Amazon — poor reviews suppress the listing's ability to convert and rank.
caveats: The ~$100 inspection price is the presenter's stated figure and will vary by supplier, city and inspection scope.
No QC method removes all defect risk; inspection reduces, not eliminates, the chance of a bad batch.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Title and bullet keyword construction for Amazon search
cards.summary: How to research search phrases and build an Amazon title where the exact primary search phrase appears first.
cards.use_when: Writing or rewriting an Amazon product title, bullet points and description for a new or underperforming listing.
steps: Identify the exact phrase a buyer would type to find your specific product and put it as the first words of the title. In the source example, the assistant initially wrote "berberine supreme herbal tea", and the presenter changed it to "berberine tea" first because ~1,200 people per month search that exact phrase and no product on Amazon matched it.
Use a keyword tool such as Helium 10 (Magnet or Cerebro) to get real search volumes and related phrases; verify the current tool interface and free/paid feature split before relying on it.

Filter the tool's suggestions into three buckets: (a) exact-match core phrases you must rank for, (b) specific supporting phrases that describe real attributes of your product (e.g. immune support, glucose, antioxidant, caffeine-free, organic), and (c) generic terms (health, wellness, energy, cardiovascular, metabolism) that are too broad to rank for and waste title space.

Mine competitor listings for phrases you may have missed — the source found "glucose support", "high strength" and "HCL" by reading berberine supplement listings, even though those products are not tea.
Put the primary phrase in the title, repeat supporting keywords naturally in the bullets and description, and understand that Amazon treats your listing text as the only way it knows what you sell.
Remember the click decision is made from title, main image, price and review count — so the title must both contain the keyword and be readable enough to earn the click.
caveats: Generic high-volume terms were rejected by the presenter because a small new listing cannot rank for them; this is his judgment, not a rule.
Keyword volumes and tool pricing change — re-verify data before committing to title terms.

cards.title: Amazon listing setup mechanics: existing listing vs. new listing
cards.summary: Step-by-step path through Seller Central for adding a product to an existing ASIN versus creating a brand-new listing.
cards.use_when: Setting up a new product in Amazon Seller Central, or choosing between piggybacking on an existing ASIN and building your own.
steps: Register at sell.amazon.com, then log into Seller Central; open the menu, go to Catalog, then Add Products (verify the current menu labels, which change).

If the product already exists on Amazon, search by name or product ID (UPC/EAN/ISBN/ASIN), pick the matching listing, select condition, click Sell this product, then enter an optional SKU, quantity, price and fulfillment channel.

If the product does not exist on Amazon, choose the blank-form/start-new-listing option and fill in item name (title), product type/category, item type keyword, variation status, brand name and external product ID.

Choose a category by looking at where similar products are actually listed — scroll to the bottom of a competitor's detail page to see their category, then match it. The presenter also mentions the advanced tactic of listing in a slightly-off subcategory where you can become the number one product, but treats it as advanced rather than default.
Decide variations up front: if you sell one flavor, size or color, answer No; if you will sell multiple flavors or sizes, answer Yes and structure them as variations.

Sourcing details to have ready: a legitimate GS1 barcode (gs1.org; the presenter notes a single barcode is about $30 versus the older ~$250 ten-pack), your brand name, and a trademark case number if you intend to use Brand Registry.
caveats: Menu paths, field names and the private-seller/condition options in Seller Central change over time — verify the current interface.
The source says to avoid unofficial barcode resellers because cheap codes can cause problems later; this is his recommendation.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Choosing FBA over merchant-fulfilled for Prime eligibility
cards.summary: Why sending inventory into Amazon's warehouses changes who ships and whether your listing can be bought by Prime customers.
cards.use_when: Deciding the fulfillment channel for a new Amazon listing, or comparing the cost of FBA fees against the sales benefit of Prime eligibility.
steps: Compare the two channels directly: with FBM (Fulfilled by Merchant) you receive the order, pack it and ship it yourself; with FBA (Fulfilled by Amazon) you send inventory to an Amazon warehouse and Amazon picks, packs and ships each order.

Weigh the FBA fee against the sales effect the source claims: FBA makes your product Prime eligible, and the presenter cites over 300 million Prime customers worldwide who pay annually for two-day shipping and prefer buying Prime products.
Select the FBA option in Seller Central so Amazon handles shipping and customer service, then complete the listing and send inventory in.
Consider operational leverage beyond the fee: with FBA you are not packing orders yourself, so the business keeps running when you travel or work elsewhere.
caveats: The 300 million Prime customer figure is the presenter's claim and will change over time.
FBA also brings its own constraints — storage costs, receiving rules and compliance requirements are not covered in this passage; check current Amazon policy.
FBA pick-and-pack fees were a major cost line in the case study (~$1,200 in a ~$9,500 month), so the Prime benefit must be weighed against real fee levels.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Using Amazon ads and promo-clear listings to relaunch a stalled product
cards.summary: How the case-study seller used PPC, A+ content and a competitor's removal to jump from a stockout toward a record month.
cards.use_when: Planning a relaunch or ranking push after a stockout, or deciding how much ad spend to reinvest into an existing Amazon listing.
steps: Reinvest profit into PPC (pay-per-click) rather than treating ad spend as pure cost: the source seller spent roughly $2,000–$3,000 on PPC in the month he grew revenue from a depleted position to about $23,000.
Improve conversion assets at the same time as buying traffic — the seller also invested in A+ content on the listing in that same month, so traffic and conversion were worked together.

Watch the competitive set for structural openings: the seller's main competitor's listing was taken down, and he took advantage of the freed demand. The source does not explain why the competitor was removed and no cause should be assumed.
Expect the ad spike to interact with inventory: that $23,000 month was followed by a stockout-driven fall to $9,000 and then ~$3,000, so a relaunch push only pays if supply supports it.
caveats: The source does not attribute the $23,000 month solely to PPC — a competitor's removal was a co-factor.
Ad budgets, campaign types and A+ eligibility rules on Amazon change; verify current requirements.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Launch speed and review momentum as copycat defense
cards.summary: Why a fast, review-generating launch is presented as protection against manufacturers copying your product.
cards.use_when: Planning the launch timeline and early review-generation push for a new private-label product, or deciding whether to delay a launch.
steps: Treat speed as a defense: the source describes a student pair whose product was copied by manufacturers a few months after a quiet launch, and says a big launch with a strong review base would have made the copy less damaging because they would have been far ahead.
Execute a large social media and launch push at launch rather than trickling in, so the listing accumulates reviews and ranking early.
Use the accumulated review advantage as the barrier — on Amazon, the source frames reviews as currency and early momentum as the thing a later copycat cannot easily match.
Pair this with formal protection (trademark/brand registry) rather than relying on launch speed alone.
caveats: This is the presenter's interpretation of what would have happened in one student's case; no measured comparison is provided.
Amazon's review-solicitation rules restrict how reviews can be requested — launch tactics must comply with current policy.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Choosing a legal entity structure for a product business (DBA, LLC, S-corp election)
cards.summary: Comparison of DBA, LLC and S-corp structures and the source's recommended hybrid: an LLC taxed as an S-corp.
cards.use_when: Forming the legal entity for a new Amazon or ecommerce store, or deciding whether a new product line needs its own entity.
steps: Compare the options on protection and cost: a DBA (doing business as) is the cheapest and fastest (around $99 via services like LegalZoom, ~15 minutes of paperwork) but gives no liability protection and cannot sell shares; the presenter recommends it mainly when the chance of being sued is low.

Choose an LLC when you need personal-asset protection — the source specifically points to consumable products or anything that could harm a customer. Costs range from about $180 to $800+ depending on the state, and the presenter pays $800/year in California even at zero revenue, with the cost rising as revenue grows.

Consider the S-corp election if tax savings matter, accepting the extra filings and formalities; the presenter notes S-corp status lets you take a reasonable salary and treat additional profit as a shareholder distribution not subject to Social Security and Medicare tax.
Use the hybrid the presenter actually recommends: form an LLC and elect S-corp taxation via a checkbox on the LLC filing, avoiding much of the standalone S-corp paperwork.
Reuse an existing entity rather than forming a new one for each product: the presenter launched a new product under his existing LLC as an umbrella, which is what he did for his electrolytes product.
If you are outside the US and want a US LLC, the presenter mentions wyregisteredagent.com at around $149.
caveats: This is business-formation guidance from a course presenter, not legal or tax advice; entity rules, state fees and S-corp requirements vary and should be confirmed with a professional.
The listed prices and service recommendations are as stated in the source and go stale.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: EIN, seller's permit and separating business banking
cards.summary: The free federal and state registrations an online seller needs, plus why commingling business and personal money is risky.
cards.use_when: Setting up back-office paperwork before launching an Amazon store, or fixing banking hygiene after mixing personal and business spending.
steps: Get an EIN directly from irs.gov: the source says it is free, takes roughly 10–15 minutes, and returns a PDF — do not pay third parties for this.

Get a seller's permit from your state, found by searching your state name plus "seller's permit" and using the official .gov site. The presenter says it is free and that anyone charging for it is running a scam.
Use the seller's permit for two things it enables: buying goods tax-free for resale (ingredients and packaging in the source's example), and filing state sales tax.

Understand the sales-tax scope the presenter describes: for online sales you collect state sales tax only from buyers in the state where you or the business resides, and larger businesses with physical locations collect in each of those states. He explicitly notes he is not a lawyer and the reality is more complicated.
Open a business bank account with the entity, EIN and permit paperwork; the presenter does this online now rather than in branch, and mentions Payoneer or WorldFirst for sellers outside the US.

Keep personal and business spending strictly separate: the presenter says commingling is an IRS red flag, can let a litigant pierce the LLC and reach personal assets, and makes it impossible to see your true profit.
caveats: The tax-scope explanation is the presenter's non-lawyer understanding; consult a professional for nexus and sales-tax obligations, especially as you add states or marketplaces.
Fee statements and agency options reflect the source's date and location.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Funding launch spend with business credit card sign-up bonuses
cards.summary: How the source turns unavoidable launch costs into travel points by routing spend through a new business card.
cards.use_when: Choosing how to pay for a product business's build-out costs (inventory, ads, samples, tooling) to maximize rewards.
steps: Match the card to your biggest spend category: the presenter recommends a card offering 5x points on advertising spend when ad spend is your largest line, noting the annual fee was a little over $100 and that the points outweighed it for him.

Consider a flat-rate card for general spend if your costs are spread across inventory, software and shipping; the presenter cites one card at 2x points on every dollar with no first-year fee and $95 thereafter.

Target the sign-up bonus threshold with legitimate business spend: the presenter says bonuses commonly require around $3,000 spend in three months, and that this is easy to hit when buying inventory and running ads.
Example from the source: roughly $5,000 of spend to start the electrolytes business, combined with sign-up bonuses, was enough for a round-trip flight to South America, Europe or Asia.
Charge business costs to the business card, not a personal card, so the spend stays traceable and separate from personal finances.
caveats: Rewards, bonus thresholds, annual fees and card availability change frequently and are not guaranteed — verify current terms.
The presenter's travel-value claim is his own experience, not a promise.
Carrying a balance to chase points costs more than the points are worth; the source's framing assumes paying the statement in full.
cards.source_name: FREE Amazon FBA Course _ 12 Hour FULL Step by Step Tutorial 2025.docx

cards.title: Trademark vs patent: which protection actually fits a private-label product
cards.summary: Choosing between trademark (design or word mark) and patent (utility or design) for an Amazon product, including the source's cost figures.
cards.use_when: Deciding what intellectual property to file before applying for Amazon Brand Registry, or protecting a product design from copycats.
steps: Decide what you are actually protecting. A utility patent covers a genuinely new invention; a design patent covers the unique look of a product (the presenter's example is the contoured Coca-Cola bottle, shape only); a trademark covers brand identifiers — your logo, font or the words themselves.

Know the cost ladder before filing: the source lists utility patent fees of a $540 search fee, $220 examination fee and $330 filing fee, plus approximately $10,000 if you hire a patent lawyer; he notes one student filed his own utility patent but said he might pay a lawyer if he did it again.
If you have an invention, the presenter's minimum recommendation is a provisional patent at about $75, which is cheap and easy and preserves the option to file a full utility patent later.
For most private-label sellers, trademark is the relevant filing: file yourself at uspto.gov (the source cites roughly $250), then submit the case number to Amazon Brand Registry.

Choose your trademark type based on purpose: the presenter says a design mark is easier to obtain and is what he'd generally use for Brand Registry, while a word mark gives broader protection (nobody else may use the words) but is harder and more strictly examined.

Skip patents when your product is not a new invention. In the source's example, an electrolyte powder was not patented because it is not novel — only the design was distinctive, which is trademark territory.
caveats: Filing fees, examination standards and Brand Registry requirements change; verify on uspto.gov and Amazon's Brand Registry page.
The $10,000 lawyer figure and $75 provisional figure are the presenter's stated numbers, not quotes.
The presenter says his product was not patented and gives no evidence that trademark alone stopped copying.

cards.title: Choosing an Amazon category and item type for your listing
cards.summary: How to pick the category and item-type keyword that determines where your product can rank.
cards.use_when: Filling in the category and item type fields while creating a new Amazon listing, or reconsidering the category of an existing listing.
steps: Let Amazon's auto-suggestion start you off, then override it if it is not specific enough: in the source, Amazon auto-selected "herbal supplement" for a tea, and the presenter changed it to the herbal tea subcategory he judged the best fit.
Validate your choice against competitors: open similar products on Amazon, scroll to the bottom of the detail page, see which category they are listed in, and match it.

Consider the advanced tactic the presenter mentions: listing in a subcategory that is not a perfect match when you believe you can become the number one product there. He flags this as an advanced decision, not a default.
Set the item type keyword that Amazon derives from the category chain, and confirm the variation setting — one flavor or size means No variations; multiple flavors, sizes or colors means Yes.

Recognize the stakes: the presenter states the number one search result takes most sales, with second through fourth well behind, and that a product off page one gets essentially no sales — so category and keyword placement decide whether you can appear at all.
caveats: Category best-fit and ranking effects vary by product and change with Amazon's browse node structure.
Category-drift tactics can restrict certain features or invite a category correction by Amazon; the source does not cover those enforcement risks.

cards.title: Reading keyword lists critically: choose specific buyer language over generic buzzwords
cards.summary: A filtering method for turning a raw keyword list into title and bullet terms that can actually rank.
cards.use_when: Editing a keyword list before writing Amazon title, bullets or description copy.
steps: Take the raw export from your keyword tool and mark each term against three questions: does it describe my exact product, is it specific enough that a small listing could rank, and is it something a buyer with purchase intent would type?

Reject broad terms per the source's example: metabolism, energy, cardiovascular, cholesterol, health, wellness and detox were set aside as too generic to rank for; herbal tea was judged good but very competitive, so a more specific variant is preferable.

Keep terms that are both searched and true of the product — in the source, immune support (~9,700 searches/month claimed), antioxidant, organic, caffeine-free, glucose/glucose support, and the product's own name.

Add terms your product actually supports even if you may not rank for them, because they still help buyers recognize the product's fit — the presenter kept "caffeine free" in the title knowing he would not rank first for it.
Combine the surviving phrases into a readable title with the primary exact phrase first, then carry the rest into bullet points and the description.
Do the same filtering on competitor listings: extract the phrases they emphasize ("high strength", "HCL", "glucose support") and check whether each applies to your product before borrowing it.
caveats: Search volumes and which terms are 'too generic' are the presenter's judgments and shift by niche and time.
Borrowing competitor keywords does not mean copying their claims — only apply terms that are accurate for your product.
